beliefs.practice: Never commit the DocumentDB/MongoDB connection string or primary key to source control; read it at runtime from an environment variable (e.g., DOCUMENTDB_URI) and do not log its value.
Prefer retrieving database credentials from a secret-store (Azure Key Vault or Managed Identity) at runtime rather than placing long-lived secrets in environment variables or files.
Require TLS/SSL for the driver connection (e.g., include tls=true or tls=true&tlsAllowInvalidCertificates=false in the Mongo URI) and reject insecure connections.

Reuse pooled connections instead of opening a new client per request: configure driver pool settings (e.g., maxPoolSize, minPoolSize, maxIdleTimeMS) and create one global client/Beanie motor client per process.
Ensure the MongoDB driver version is compatible with the server wire protocol (use a driver that supports MongoDB 7.0 when the cluster advertises MongoDB 7.0).
Define clear Pydantic/Beanie models for documents (explicit fields, types, and index definitions) and use those models everywhere rather than raw dicts to keep schema consistent.

Create conventional indexes for fields used in filters/joins/aggregations (e.g., category, root_cause, urgency_tier, created_at) before running production queries so aggregations and lookups use indexes.

For similarity search, store embeddings as a fixed-length numeric array field (not a blob/string) and create a dedicated vector index with the correct dimension and distance metric (e.g., cosine or euclidean) rather than treating vectors as ordinary fields.

When creating vector indexes (HNSW / DiskANN /IVF), explicitly configure index hyperparameters (dimension, M / efConstruction / efSearch, metric) appropriate for your vector dimension and recall/latency tradeoffs and document that configuration in code.

Keep documents reasonably small: if complaint text is large, either store raw text in a separate blob store and keep a truncated version in the document or chunk long texts and store embeddings per chunk to avoid hitting document size limits and to improve search performance.
Use bulk writes (insert_many / bulk_write) with unordered operations when seeding to improve throughput; handle duplicate-key errors and be idempotent so seed scripts can be re-run safely.
Define and use idempotent update patterns for the enrichment pipeline (e.g., upsert by a stable complaint_id or use a processed flag) to avoid double-processing when retries occur.

Implement retry with exponential backoff for transient network failures; distinguish idempotent vs non-idempotent operations and only auto-retry idempotent operations (or use transaction boundaries / two-phase updates for non-idempotent ones).

Use aggregation pipelines on the server (e.g., $group, $sort, $limit, $bucket) to compute complaint hotspots by category rather than pulling all documents into the app; ensure grouping fields are indexed to optimize the aggregation.

Avoid low-cardinality fields as shard/partition keys (e.g., 'category' may be too low-cardinality); choose a high-cardinality partition key or use hashed keys to distribute load evenly for large collections.

If the cluster exposes configurable throughput or instance sizes, monitor and scale provisioned resources (compute tier, RU/s or instance size) to meet latency/throughput needs, and use autoscale where available for production workloads.

When performing similarity search, normalize vectors before choosing a metric: if using cosine distance normalize vectors and then use inner-product/Euclidean depending on the engine; document which metric aligns to your embeddings.
Limit the number of results returned from similarity queries (k) and paginate results; avoid scanning the whole collection in the application layer for nearest-neighbor search.

Define indexes (and index-creation helpers/scripts) to be idempotent: use createIndex with the same index spec and handle 'index already exists' errors gracefully so deploy scripts are safe to re-run.
Use partial or sparse indexes for fields that are often missing (e.g., processed_flag, urgency_tier) to reduce index size and improve write performance if queries filter on those fields.
Protect PII by encrypting sensitive fields at rest (use Azure-managed encryption or customer-managed keys) and consider client-side field-level encryption for highly sensitive data.

Cache embeddings and classification results for identical or near-duplicate complaint texts to avoid repeated LLM/embedding calls; store cache keys (e.g., text hash) alongside documents or in a separate cache store.
Instrument and monitor slow queries and index usage (profiling or APM); add alerts for high latency, high error-rate operations, and high memory usage of vector indexes.
Use optimistic concurrency control (e.g., include a version or updated_at field and check it on update) when enriching documents concurrently to prevent lost updates.

Keep deployment and test workflows safe: unit tests should use a local or test database and never run destructive write operations against a production cluster; seed scripts should be guarded and require an explicit flag/confirmation.
